core.title: Error responses carry a structured, coded payload, never a bare string literal body
core.given: Non-test source contains an error response: a response carrying a client-error or server-error status (4xx/5xx)
core.when: that error response's body is a bare string literal, whether the body or the status was the part written or changed
core.then: The error response MUST carry a structured payload with an error code, not a bare string literal body.
prefer: The boundary returns a coded, structured payload for the error and renders any user-facing fragment separately.
avoid: A bare string literal as the body of an error response returned by the boundary.
unless: The response status is 2xx or 3xx (out of scope).
The body is a variable or a rendered fragment, which is not a bare literal.
The code is in a test file.
core.why: Where the stack's presentation client renders the response body into the page the user sees, a bare error string is not merely unstructured data a client must parse but content rendered to the user verbatim, including whatever internal detail it carries (a stack frame, a table name, an upstream message); the structured payload is both the machine-readable contract and the boundary that stops internals leaking into the page. This is sharper where bodies are rendered into the live page than in a pure JSON API, which is why it is enforced rather than advised.
evidence: The stack's convention check reports no finding of this rule (an error response with a bare string literal body) on changed non-test files.

Reviewer sees no changed non-test error response with a bare string literal body; where a literal body was replaced, it is a structured payload with an error code. Bodies that are variables or rendered fragments are not in scope.
verification: Severity 4; strict disposition: the rule fails on every finding; it is enforced, not advisory.

A stack check flags an error response (a response with a 4xx/5xx status) whose body is a bare string literal; the exact syntactic pattern matched (the stack's response construct and its literal body form) is a realization detail of the stack's checker.

The check does not flag: responses with a 2xx or 3xx status, whatever their body; error responses whose body argument is a variable, an identifier, or a rendered fragment (any non-literal expression); or code in test files. Which files count as test files follows the stack's profile and the checker's classification, exactly as the reference realization defers it.

fires: Non-test source returns an error response (a 4xx/5xx status) whose body is a bare string literal, whatever the status value.
A change sets the status of a response with a string-literal body from a success or redirect status to an error status (status-only change).
doesNotFire: A response with a 2xx or 3xx status, whatever its body.
An error response whose body is a variable or a rendered fragment.

profileRequirements.meaning: The stack's response construct for a response carrying an error status, and its form of a structured, serialized payload body: the concrete referents of the core's 'error response (a response with a 4xx/5xx status)' and 'structured payload with an error code'. Only stack data lives here; this rule's literal-body detection pattern and worked example stay in the realization.
profileRequirements.bunValue: A response is the web-standard `Response` object: `new Response(<body>, { status })` returns a raw body, `Response.json(<payload>, { status })` serializes a structured payload as the response body.

proposedKeys.meaning: How the stack constructs a response carrying an error status, and how a structured, serialized payload is returned as that response's body — the concrete referents of a core's 'error response (a response with a 4xx/5xx status)' and 'structured payload with an error code'. Stack data only; a rule's detection patterns and worked examples stay with the rule's realization.
proposedKeys.bunValue: A response is the web-standard `Response` object: `new Response(<body>, { status })` returns a raw body, `Response.json(<payload>, { status })` serializes a structured payload as the response body.
proposedKeys.whyNoExistingKey: idiom.error_types is documented as how domain and boundary errors are typed and raised — not HTTP response construction or body serialization — and repurposing it was rejected in audit r2; no other idiom key (route_handler, validation_shape, dto_mapper_naming) describes how a response is built or how a payload is serialized as its body.

neutralityNotes: HTTP status classes (4xx/5xx, 2xx/3xx) are kept in the core: they are protocol-level facts shared by every realization of this obligation family (both the Bun and the python-pytest sibling speak HTTP statuses), not stack, runtime or framework names; the concrete construct that carries a status comes from the proposed profile key idiom.error_response_payload. 'Bare string literal' is kept as a cross-stack syntactic notion — both known realizations flag string literals — while each stack's checker defines the exact literal forms (the Bun pattern stays in the realization, not the profile). The htmx-specific rationale is generalized to 'the presentation client renders the response body into the page the user sees'; the concrete mechanism (htmx swapping into the live DOM) is preserved in bun.json and the bunOnly entry for verifier_detail[5]. What counts as a test file is not pinned in the core: the Bun text itself defers the exclusion to its checker, so the core keeps that deference in verification. Per audit r2 feedback, idiom.error_types is no longer used: it means how domain and boundary errors are typed and raised, not response construction or payload serialization. The core does need profile data for response/payload construction, so a narrowly defined idiom key (idiom.error_response_payload) is proposed, carrying only stack data; this rule's flagging condition (first argument a string literal, status 400–599) and its worked example remain in the Bun realization and its bunOnly entries. tooling.languages covers the language fact; nothing else was missing.
